title: Tempestas. Acestes. Anguis in tumulo
titleEn: The Storm, Acestes and the Serpent at the Tomb — Aeneid V.1–103
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Book V opens at sea. Aeneas has left Carthage behind and holds a steady course, but looking back he sees the city lit by flames, and no one on board knows what lit them; the Trojans guess, from their old grief and from what a woman in a frenzy can do, that it is Dido's pyre. Out of sight of land a black storm gathers, and the helmsman Palinurus warns that no one could hope to reach Italy under such a sky. Aeneas agrees to turn for Sicily, where Eryx, his half-brother, once held the coast and where his father Anchises lies buried: the bones are in the earth there, and Acestes, a king of Trojan blood, rules the land. Acestes comes running down from a mountain top, dressed in a bearskin and bristling with javelins, and welcomes the Trojans home with country gifts. At dawn Aeneas calls his men to the burial mound and announces that a year has passed since they laid his father to rest: on the ninth day from now he will hold games in Anchises' honour, with foot races, boxing, archery and contests of strength for ships' crews. He wreathes his head with myrtle, the others follow, and he pours wine, milk and blood on the grave and scatters purple flowers. Then a snake, huge, coiled seven times and shining like a rainbow, glides out from the depths of the tomb, tastes the offerings and slips back inside. Aeneas cannot tell whether it is the guardian spirit of the place or his father's attendant, and he goes on with the sacrifice and the feast. Virgil is again working with Homer in view, the Odyssey's sea-voyages and the Iliad's funeral games for Patroclus, which Book V will rewrite in Roman terms.
part: The Storm, Acestes and the Serpent at the Tomb (V.1–103)

sentences.t:
Interea medium Aeneas iam classe tenebat
certus iter, fluctusque atros Aquilone secabat,
moenia respiciens, quae iam infelicis Elissae
conlucent flammis.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the middle, Aeneas now with his fleet, was holding
sure, the way, and the dark waves with the North wind was cutting,
the walls looking back at, which now of unhappy Elissa
are gleaming with flames.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Aeneas, with his fleet well out on the open sea, was holding a sure course and cutting the dark waves with the north wind, looking back at the walls that now gleamed with the flames of unhappy Elissa.
sentences.n: Book V opens in the middle of the voyage; the departure from Carthage was told at the end of Book IV. 'medium' (line 1) agrees with 'iter' (line 2), which is the object of 'tenebat', 'was holding': 'the midway course', i.e. the open sea; the noun is held back to the next line. 'certus' is nominative, 'sure (of his way)'. 'classe' and 'Aquilone' are ablatives, 'with his fleet' and 'with the north wind'. 'moenia respiciens' is a present participle, 'looking back at the walls'. 'quae… conlucent' is a relative clause: 'conlucere' means 'to shine all over, gleam'. 'Elissae' is genitive; Elissa is Dido's other name. The 'flames' are Dido's funeral pyre, whose cause the Trojans do not know: the next lines say so.

sentences.t:
Quae tantum accenderit ignem,
causa latet;
sentences.l:
What so great a fire has kindled,
the cause lies hidden;
sentences.i: The cause that kindled so great a fire is hidden from them;
sentences.n: 'quae… causa' is one phrase broken up by the verse: 'what cause kindled so great a fire'. It is an indirect question, so 'accenderit' is a perfect subjunctive, and the whole question is the subject of 'latet'. 'tantum' agrees with 'ignem', 'so great a fire' (it is not an adverb here). The narrator knows the answer (Dido's suicide), the Trojans do not.

sentences.t:
duri magno sed amore dolores
polluto, notumque, furens quid femina possit,
triste per augurium Teucrorum pectora ducunt.
sentences.l:
but hard pangs, a great love
defiled, and the known thing, what a woman raving may do,
through a sad presage lead the hearts of the Teucrians.
sentences.i: but the bitter pain of a great love betrayed, and the knowledge of what a woman in her frenzy can do, lead the hearts of the Trojans down a path of sad foreboding.
sentences.n: 'sed' is postponed to the third place in its clause, as Latin allows. 'duri… dolores' is the subject of 'ducunt' and 'Teucrorum pectora' the object; 'magno… amore polluto' is an ablative absolute, 'a great love having been defiled'. 'notum' is a neuter participle used as a noun, 'the known (thing)', with the indirect question 'furens quid femina possit' (present subjunctive) in apposition to it; 'furens' is a present participle, 'raving'. 'Teucrorum' is a genitive plural (Teucri is another word for the Trojans, from their ancestor Teucer). 'per augurium' means 'through a presage'; 'ducunt' here means 'lead' or 'draw', the hearts being led towards a forecast.

sentences.t:
Ut pelagus tenuere rates, nec iam amplius ulla
occurrit tellus, maria undique et undique caelum,
sentences.l:
When the sea the ships had gained, and now no longer any
land appears, seas on every side and on every side the sky,
sentences.i: When the ships had reached the open sea, and no land showed any more, and there was water on every side and sky on every side,
sentences.n: 'Ut' with the perfect indicative 'tenuere' means 'when'; 'tenuere' is the form in -ere for 'tenuerunt' (you'll see this constantly). 'pelagus' is a neuter noun (a Greek loanword) in the accusative, 'the open sea'. 'nec iam amplius ulla… tellus' is 'and no land any longer'. 'maria undique et undique caelum' is a verbless phrase in the nominative, the repeated 'undique' (from every side) closing the Trojans in with nothing but water and sky.

sentences.t:
olli caeruleus supra caput adstitit imber,
noctem hiememque ferens, et inhorruit unda tenebris.
sentences.l:
over his head stood a dark-blue storm-cloud,
bringing night and winter, and the wave bristled with the darkness.
sentences.i: a dark rain-cloud stood over his head, bringing night and winter weather, and the water roughened in the gloom.
sentences.n: 'olli' is an old form of the dative 'illi', 'for him', i.e. Aeneas, with 'supra caput', 'over his head'. 'imber' is the subject of 'adstitit' ('stood'), a perfect of 'adsto'; Greenough prints 'adstitit' where The Latin Library has 'astitit', a spelling difference only. 'noctem hiememque ferens' means 'bringing night and storm'. 'inhorruit' is the perfect of 'inhorresco', 'shivered, bristled': the wave stands up in ridges. 'tenebris' is an ablative, 'with the darkness'.

sentences.t: Ipse gubernator puppi Palinurus ab alta:
sentences.l: Himself the pilot Palinurus from the high stern:
sentences.i: The helmsman himself, Palinurus, called from the high stern:
sentences.n: The speech comes after a colon; 'dixit' or the like is understood (ellipsis of the verb of speaking, as often). 'gubernator' is the helmsman, in apposition to 'Palinurus', and 'puppi… ab alta' is 'from the high stern', where the steersman stood. Palinurus is the pilot who will be lost overboard at the end of this book.

sentences.t: “Heu! quianam tanti cinxerunt aethera nimbi?
sentences.l: “Alas! why have so great clouds girt the sky?
sentences.i: “Alas! why have such great storm-clouds wrapped the heavens round?
sentences.n: The opening mark “ begins Palinurus's speech, which ends at 14. 'Heu' is an exclamation of dismay. 'quianam' is an emphatic 'why', an old word. 'cinxerunt' is a perfect, 'have encircled', of 'cingo'; 'aethera' is the Greek accusative singular of 'aether', 'the upper air'; 'tanti… nimbi' is nominative plural, 'such great clouds'.

sentences.t: Quidve, pater Neptune, paras?
sentences.l: Or what, father Neptune, are you preparing?”
sentences.i: What is it, father Neptune, that you are preparing?”
sentences.n: 'Quid' with the enclitic '-ve' means 'or what?'. 'pater Neptune' is a vocative: Palinurus addresses the sea-god directly. The closing mark ” appears in Greenough's printing after the question mark, with a space before it, and in front of 'Sic' on the same line; the cut keeps it with the question it closes.

sentences.t:
”Sic deinde locutus
colligere arma iubet validisque incumbere remis,
obliquatque sinus in ventum, ac talia fatur:
sentences.l:
Thus then having spoken
he orders to gather the gear and to bend to the strong oars,
and slants the sails to the wind, and such things says:
sentences.i: Having spoken so, he orders the rigging taken in and the men to bend to their stout oars, and he trims the sails to catch the wind, and says:
sentences.n: 'locutus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'loquor', active in sense: 'having spoken'. 'iubet' takes the accusative-and-infinitive; the infinitives 'colligere' and 'incumbere' have the crew as understood subject. 'arma' here means the ship's gear, the 'tackle' (sails and rigging). 'validis… remis' is a dative with 'incumbere', 'lean on the strong oars'. 'obliquat sinus in ventum' means 'turns the folds of the sail slantwise to the wind'. 'ac talia fatur' (a formula) 'and such things he says'; 'fatur' is deponent.

sentences.t:
“Magnanime Aenea, non, si mihi Iuppiter auctor
spondeat, hoc sperem Italiam contingere caelo.
sentences.l:
“Great-hearted Aeneas, not if Jupiter to me as guarantor
were to pledge, could I hope to touch Italy under this sky.
sentences.i: “Great-souled Aeneas, not if Jupiter were to stand surety and give me his word could I hope to reach Italy under a sky like this.
sentences.n: 'Magnanime Aenea' is a vocative; 'Aenea' is the Greek-style vocative. 'si… spondeat' is a present subjunctive condition ('if Jupiter should vouch'), and 'non… sperem' is the present subjunctive of the apodosis, a potential ('I could not hope'). 'mihi' is a dative with 'spondeat' and 'auctor' is predicative, 'as guarantor'. 'Italiam contingere' is the accusative-and-infinitive after 'sperem'. 'hoc… caelo' is an ablative of attendant circumstance, 'under this sky'.

sentences.t:
Mutati transversa fremunt et vespere ab atro
consurgunt venti, atque in nubem cogitur aër.
sentences.l:
The changed winds roar athwart, and from the dark west
rise up, and into a cloud is the air gathered.
sentences.i: The winds have shifted and roar across our course, rising from the black western sky, and the air is packed into one great cloud.
sentences.n: 'Mutati' is a perfect participle agreeing with 'venti': 'changed, having shifted'. 'transversa' is a neuter plural used as an adverb, 'across, athwart'. 'vespere ab atro' means 'from the dark evening', i.e. the west. 'consurgunt' is plural to agree with 'venti'. 'aër' is the nominative of the Greek loanword 'aer', 'air'; Greenough's diaeresis marks two syllables (a-er), and The Latin Library prints it without, which makes no difference to the sense. 'cogitur' is a passive, 'is driven together'.

sentences.t:
Nec nos obniti contra, nec tendere tantum
sufficimus.
sentences.l:
Nor to strive against it, nor to strain so much
are we able.
sentences.i: We have not strength to push against it, nor to strain hard enough.
sentences.n: 'sufficimus' takes the two infinitives 'obniti' and 'tendere', 'we are able to strive, to strain'. 'nec… nec' is the correlative pair 'neither… nor'. 'obniti' is the infinitive of the deponent 'obnitor', 'push against'. 'tantum' is an adverb, 'so much'. The verb ends the unit, after the line break.

sentences.t:
Superat quoniam Fortuna, sequamur,
quoque vocat, vertamus iter.
sentences.l:
Since Fortune prevails, let us follow,
and wherever she calls, let us turn our course.
sentences.i: Since Fortune has the mastery, let us go with her, and turn our course wherever she calls.
sentences.n: 'Superat' is used absolutely, 'prevails'; 'quoniam' is 'since'. 'sequamur' and 'vertamus' are present subjunctives, hortatory ('let us…'). 'quo' is the relative adverb 'whither', with the '-que' joining the two halves: 'and whither she calls'. 'Fortuna' is capitalised by Greenough, treated as a divinity.

sentences.t:
Nec litora longe
fida reor fraterna Erycis portusque Sicanos,
si modo rite memor servata remetior astra.”
sentences.l:
Nor shores far off
trusty do I think, the fraternal of Eryx, and the Sicanian harbours,
if only rightly mindful I measure back the stars observed.”
sentences.i: And I think the shores of Eryx, your brother's land, and the Sicilian harbours lie not far off and are safe, if I truly remember the stars I watched and can measure my course back by them.”
sentences.n: 'reor' takes an accusative and infinitive with 'esse' understood: 'litora… fida (esse) reor', 'I think the shores are trustworthy'. 'nec… longe' goes with 'reor': 'I do not think them far off'; 'fida' adds 'safe, trustworthy'. 'fraterna Erycis' means 'of your brother Eryx': Eryx was a son of Venus, and so Aeneas's half-brother, and gave his name to the Sicilian mountain and kingdom. 'Sicanos' means Sicilian (the Sicani are an old people of the island). 'si modo… memor… remetior' means 'if only I am mindful in measuring back'; 'remetior' is deponent, 'measure again', and 'servata… astra' are the stars watched on the outward course. The closing mark ” ends Palinurus's second speech.

sentences.t: Tum pius Aeneas:
sentences.l: Then good Aeneas:
sentences.i: Then dutiful Aeneas answered:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'pius' is Aeneas's constant epithet: it means dutiful towards gods, family and country. The verb of speaking is again left out (ellipsis).

sentences.t:
“Equidem sic poscere ventos
iamdudum et frustra cerno te tendere contra:
sentences.l:
“Indeed so to demand, the winds,
long ago and in vain I see, you strain against them:
sentences.i: “I have seen for some time now that this is what the winds demand, and that you strain against them in vain.
sentences.n: 'Equidem' is 'for my part, indeed'. 'cerno' governs two accusative-and-infinitive clauses: 'ventos… sic poscere', in which 'ventos' is the subject, 'that the winds demand it so', and 'te… tendere contra', 'that you strain against them'. 'sic' means 'in this way'. 'iamdudum' with a present verb means 'for a long time now'. 'tendere contra' means 'strain against (them)'.

sentences.t: Flecte viam velis.
sentences.l: Bend the course with the sails.
sentences.i: Turn our course with the sails.
sentences.n: 'Flecte' is an imperative of 'flecto'; 'velis' is an ablative of means. Palinurus has said he fears the weather and suggested a turn to the Sicilian shore; Aeneas now orders it.

sentences.t:
An sit mihi gratior ulla,
quove magis fessas optem demittere naves,
quam quae Dardanium tellus mihi servat Acesten,
et patris Anchisae gremio complectitur ossa?”
sentences.l:
Or could there be to me any land more welcome,
or to which I should rather wish to bring down my weary ships,
than that which the Dardanian Acestes keeps for me,
and in the bosom of father Anchises embraces his bones?”
sentences.i: Is there any land that could be dearer to me, or where I should rather wish to bring down my weary ships, than the land that keeps Trojan Acestes for me, and holds my father Anchises's bones in its lap?”
sentences.n: 'An sit… quove… optem' is a pair of rhetorical questions with subjunctives (a potential or deliberative use): 'could there be? or could I wish?'. 'An' without a preceding clause often introduces a question that expects 'no'. 'mihi gratior' is 'more pleasing to me'. 'demittere' is the infinitive, 'to lower, to bring down' (Greenough; The Latin Library has 'dimittere'). 'quam quae… tellus' means 'than the land which'. 'Dardanium… Acesten' is a Greek accusative (-en) with the epithet 'Dardanian', i.e. Trojan; Acestes was born in Sicily of a Trojan mother. 'servat' means 'keeps (safe) for me'; 'gremio' is an ablative of place and is the 'lap, bosom' of the earth, with 'complectitur' a deponent, 'embraces'. The mark ” closes Aeneas's speech.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi dicta, petunt portus, et vela secundi
intendunt Zephyri;
sentences.l:
These things when said, they seek the harbours, and the sails the favouring
Zephyrs stretch tight;
sentences.i: When this is said, they make for the harbours, and the kindly west winds fill out their sails;
sentences.n: 'Haec ubi dicta' has 'sunt' understood (ellipsis): 'when these things had been said'. 'portus' is the accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun (the same form as the nominative singular and plural); 'secundi Zephyri' is the subject of 'intendunt' ('stretch tight'), with 'vela' the object. 'Zephyri' are west winds; 'secundi' means 'following, favourable'.

sentences.t:
fertur cita gurgite classis,
et tandem laeti notae advertuntur harenae.
sentences.l:
is borne swiftly on the flood the fleet,
and at last glad to the known sands they are turned.
sentences.i: the fleet is carried swiftly over the water, and at last, rejoicing, they are brought round to a shore they know.
sentences.n: 'fertur' is a passive, 'is carried'. 'cita' is an adjective agreeing with 'classis'. 'gurgite' is an ablative of the way, 'over the flood'. 'laeti' is nominative plural masculine, 'glad', agreeing with the (understood) crews. 'advertuntur' is a passive used in a reflexive sense, 'turn themselves towards', with 'notae… harenae' a dative, 'to the known sands'. The sands are 'notae' because the Trojans had been in Sicily before (they buried Anchises there at the end of Book III).

sentences.t:
At procul ex celso miratus vertice montis
adventum sociasque rates occurrit Acestes,
sentences.l:
But afar, from a lofty summit of a mountain,
wondering at the arrival and the allied ships, runs to meet them Acestes,
sentences.i: But far off, from the high crest of a mountain, Acestes saw with wonder the arrival of the friendly ships and ran to meet them,
sentences.n: 'At' marks the shift of scene, and begins a new paragraph. 'miratus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'miror', which is active in sense: 'having marvelled at', with the objects 'adventum' and 'rates'. 'sociasque rates' is 'friendly ships', 'socias' agreeing with 'rates' ('rafts', here simply 'ships'). 'occurrit' is a present, 'runs to meet'; the historical present, with 'miratus' placed first and the subject 'Acestes' last in the line, delays the name.

sentences.t:
horridus in iaculis et pelle Libystidis ursae,
Troïa Criniso conceptum flumine mater
quem genuit:
sentences.l:
bristling in javelins and the skin of a Libyan she-bear,
Trojan, from the river Crinisus conceived, the mother
whom bore:
sentences.i: rough in his javelins and the pelt of a Libyan she-bear, the son whom his Trojan mother bore, conceived by the river Crinisus:
sentences.n: 'horridus' means 'bristling', 'rough', and 'in iaculis' means 'with javelins' ('in' used for the equipment worn). 'Libystidis' is the genitive of the Greek-form adjective 'Libystis', 'Libyan'. 'quem' is the relative (accusative) object of 'genuit', and 'Troïa… mater' is the subject ('Troïa' is an adjective, 'Trojan', agreeing with 'mater'), with the diaeresis showing three syllables. 'conceptum' is a perfect participle agreeing with 'quem', and 'Criniso flumine' is an ablative of source: his father was the Sicilian river-god Crinisus, who had begotten him on a Trojan woman sent to Sicily. The colon leads to the main verb in the next line.

sentences.t:
veterum non immemor ille parentum
gratatur reduces, et gaza laetus agresti
excipit, ac fessos opibus solatur amicis.
sentences.l:
of old parents not unmindful, he
congratulates them returned, and with rustic wealth glad
receives them, and tired with friendly resources comforts them.
sentences.i: Not forgetful of his ancestors, he rejoices at their return, and gladly welcomes them with the riches of the countryside, and eases their weariness with his friendly stores.
sentences.n: 'veterum… parentum' is 'of his ancestors' (not 'parents'); 'non immemor' is litotes, 'mindful'. 'gratatur' is a deponent, 'congratulates', and 'reduces' is an accusative plural: 'returned', as 'those brought back'. 'gaza laetus agresti' means 'glad with country wealth', 'gaza' being a loanword for treasure, here with a touch of irony for the farm produce. 'excipit' means 'welcomes'; 'fessos' is accusative plural (agreeing with the understood 'eos'); 'opibus amicis' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
Postera cum primo stellas Oriente fugarat
clara dies, socios in coetum litore ab omni
advocat Aeneas, tumulique ex aggere fatur:
sentences.l:
The next day, when with the first East the stars it had put to flight,
bright day, the allies to an assembly from every shore
summons Aeneas, and from the rampart of a mound says:
sentences.i: When the next day, bright with the first light of the east, had put the stars to flight, Aeneas called his comrades from every part of the shore to an assembly and spoke from the top of a mound:
sentences.n: 'Postera… clara dies' is the subject of 'fugarat', a syncopated pluperfect for 'fugaverat', after 'cum', 'when the day had put the stars to flight'. 'primo Oriente' is an ablative of time, 'at the first rising of the east'. 'in coetum' is 'into an assembly', and 'litore ab omni' 'from every shore'. 'tumuli ex aggere' means 'from the bank of a mound' (probably Anchises's tomb or a mound by it). 'fatur' is a deponent present; the speech that follows runs to line 71.

sentences.t:
“Dardanidae magni, genus alto a sanguine divom,
annuus exactis completur mensibus orbis,
sentences.l:
“Great Dardanidae, a race from the lofty blood of the gods,
the yearly circle is completed with the months run out,
sentences.i: “Great sons of Dardanus, sprung from the high blood of the gods, the circle of the year is rounding out its months,
sentences.n: 'Dardanidae' is a vocative plural, 'descendants of Dardanus', the founder of Troy. 'divom' is an old genitive plural (-om for -orum): you'll see it constantly. 'genus alto a sanguine' is in apposition to the vocative, 'a race from lofty blood'. 'exactis… mensibus' is an ablative absolute, 'the months having been completed'; 'annuus… orbis' is the nominative subject of 'completur' (a passive, 'is completed').

sentences.t:
ex quo reliquias divinique ossa parentis
Condidimus terra maestasque sacravimus aras.
sentences.l:
from when the remains and the bones of my divine parent
we buried in the earth, and sorrowing altars consecrated.
sentences.i: since the day we laid in the ground the remains and bones of my godlike father and hallowed the altars of our grief.
sentences.n: 'ex quo' is 'from the time when', with the perfect indicative. 'reliquias' is a noun, 'remains', accusative plural, and 'divini… parentis' is 'of my divine father', a genitive: Anchises, now dead, is spoken of as a sacred figure. 'Condidimus' is capitalised by Greenough after the line break; the verb has the force of 'buried, laid away'. 'maestas… aras' means 'altars (made) mournful'; 'sacravimus' is a perfect, 'consecrated'.

sentences.t:
Iamque dies, nisi fallor, adest, quem semper acerbum,
semper honoratum—sic di voluistis—habebo.
sentences.l:
And now the day, unless I am mistaken, is at hand, which always bitter,
always honoured — so, O gods, you have willed — I shall hold.
sentences.i: And now the day is here, unless I am mistaken, that I shall always hold as bitter, and always hold in honour, as you gods have willed.
sentences.n: 'quem… habebo' is a relative clause with a future verb, 'which I shall keep'; 'acerbum' and 'honoratum' are predicate adjectives, 'as bitter, as honoured'. 'sic di voluistis' is a parenthesis between dashes, 'so you gods have willed' (the contracted 'di' is vocative plural). 'nisi fallor' (passive, 'unless I am deceived') is a stock hedge.

sentences.t:
Hunc ego Gaetulis agerem si Syrtibus exsul,
Argolicove mari deprensus et urbe Mycenae;
sentences.l:
This I, if I were spending among the Gaetulian Syrtes, an exile,
or on the Argive sea caught, and in the city of Mycenae;
sentences.i: If I were spending this day as an exile among the Gaetulian quicksands, or overtaken on the Argive sea, or in the city of Mycenae itself,
sentences.n: 'si… agerem' is an imperfect subjunctive, a present contrary-to-fact condition: 'if I were spending'; the main clause is 'exsequerer… strueremque' two lines below. 'Hunc' is the object, 'this day'. 'Gaetulis Syrtibus' is an ablative of place (the Syrtes are the shifting sandbanks on the African coast, Gaetulia the land behind them). 'Argolico mari' is the sea around Argos, and 'deprensus' is a perfect participle, 'overtaken, caught' (by a storm). 'urbe Mycenae' means 'in the city of Mycenae': 'Mycenae' is taken as a genitive singular dependent on 'urbe' (a plural name would stand in the ablative as 'Mycenis'). Mycenae was the home of Agamemnon, so the very centre of Greek hostility.

sentences.t:
annua vota tamen sollemnisque ordine pompas
exsequerer, strueremque suis altaria donis.
sentences.l:
yearly vows nevertheless and solemn processions in order
I would perform, and would build the altars with their own gifts.
sentences.i: yet still I should carry out the yearly vows and the processions of the rite in due order, and heap up the altars with their proper gifts.
sentences.n: 'exsequerer' and 'strueremque' are imperfect subjunctives, the apodosis of 'si agerem': 'I should perform… and build'. 'tamen' means 'all the same'. 'sollemnis' is the -is accusative plural of 'sollemnis', agreeing with 'pompas' (Greenough's spelling for 'sollemnes'). 'ordine' is an ablative, 'in order'; 'suis… donis' means 'with their own gifts' ('suis' here means the gifts proper to them).

sentences.t:
Nunc ultro ad cineres ipsius et ossa parentis,
haud equidem sine mente, reor, sine numine divom,
adsumus et portus delati intramus amicos.
sentences.l:
Now of our own accord to the ashes of himself and the bones of my parent,
not indeed without a purpose, I think, without the divinity of the gods,
we are present, and carried into friendly harbours we enter.
sentences.i: But now, of our own accord, we stand beside the very ashes and bones of my father; not, I think, without a purpose, not without the will of the gods have we come, and, carried here, we enter friendly harbours.
sentences.n: 'ultro' means 'of our own accord, unasked'. 'ipsius' is a genitive of 'ipse' referring to Anchises, 'of himself'; 'parentis' is genitive. 'haud equidem sine mente, reor, sine numine divom' is litotes, 'not without'; 'reor' ('I think') is a parenthesis, and 'divom' is the old genitive plural. 'adsumus' (from 'adsum') is present; 'delati' is a participle, 'having been carried down' (by the winds), nominative plural. 'portus… amicos' is the object of 'intramus'; 'portus' is accusative plural (fourth declension, same form as the nominative).

sentences.t: Ergo agite, et laetum cuncti celebremus honorem;
sentences.l: Therefore come, and let us all celebrate the glad honour;
sentences.i: Come then, all of you, and let us keep this rite with gladness;
sentences.n: 'Ergo agite' means 'come, then' (an imperative idiom). 'celebremus' is a hortatory subjunctive, 'let us celebrate'. 'laetum… honorem' is 'the joyful honour', the rite itself.

sentences.t:
poscamus ventos; atque haec me sacra quotannis
urbe velit posita templis sibi ferre dicatis.
sentences.l:
let us ask for winds; and that these rites me yearly
in a city founded let him will to bring to himself in temples dedicated.
sentences.i: Let us ask for winds; and may my father be willing that, when my city is founded, I bring these rites to him every year in temples dedicated to him.
sentences.n: 'poscamus ventos' is another hortatory subjunctive, 'let us ask for (fair) winds'. 'atque haec me sacra… velit… ferre' has 'velit' as a present subjunctive (a wish, 'may he will'), with the accusative-and-infinitive 'me… ferre'. The subject of 'velit' is not stated; 'sibi' ('to himself') refers back to it, and the sense requires Anchises: 'may he (my father) be willing'. 'urbe posita' is an ablative absolute, 'the city having been founded'; 'templis dicatis' is an ablative of place with a participle, 'in temples dedicated (to him)'. 'quotannis' means 'every year'.

sentences.t:
Bina boum vobis Troia generatus Acestes
dat numero capita in naves; adhibete Penates
et patrios epulis et quos colit hospes Acestes.
sentences.l:
Two of oxen for you, born of Troy, Acestes
gives by number heads for the ships; invite the Penates
ancestral to the feasts and those whom the host Acestes worships.
sentences.i: Acestes, born of Troy, gives you two head of cattle for each ship; bring to the banquet your ancestral household gods, and those that our host Acestes worships.
sentences.n: 'Bina' is a distributive numeral, 'two each'; 'boum' is the genitive plural of 'bos' ('of oxen') and 'capita' the accusative, 'two heads of cattle'; 'numero' is an ablative, 'by count'. 'vobis' is a dative, 'for you'; 'in naves' means 'for the ships' (Greenough prints 'naves'; The Latin Library prints the -is accusative 'nauis', no change of sense). 'Troia generatus' is an ablative of origin, 'born of Troy'. 'adhibete' is an imperative, 'invite, bring in'; 'Penates' is the accusative plural (the household gods) with 'patrios', 'ancestral', and 'epulis' is a dative, 'to the feasts'. 'quos colit hospes Acestes' means the local gods of Acestes's land; 'hospes' is a noun, 'host'.

sentences.i: And furthermore, when the ninth dawn has brought out the day that gives life to men and uncovered the world with her beams, I will set for the Trojans first the contests of the swift ships;
sentences.n: 'si… extulerit radiisque retexerit' is a future perfect pair, 'if (when) she shall have brought out… and uncovered'. 'nona' agrees with 'Aurora' in the next line (not with 'diem'): 'the ninth dawn'; 'diem mortalibus almum' is the object of 'extulerit', 'a day kind to mortals'. 'retexerit orbem' means 'unweave, uncover'. 'ponam' is a future, 'I will set, establish'; 'prima' is an adjective meaning 'first of all'; 'Teucris' is a dative, 'for the Trojans'. 'citae… classis' is a genitive, 'of the swift fleet': the ship race is the first contest.

sentences.t:
quique pedum cursu valet, et qui viribus audax
aut iaculo incedit melior levibusque sagittis,
sentences.l:
and whoever in the running of feet is strong, and he who bold in strength
or with the javelin advances better and with light arrows,
sentences.i: and whoever is strong in the foot-race, and whoever steps forward bold in his strength, or better with the javelin and the light arrows,
sentences.n: 'quique… valet' is 'and whoever is strong', and the relative with 'qui' repeated: 'qui… valet, et qui… incedit'. 'pedum cursu' is an ablative of respect, 'in running of feet'. 'viribus audax' means 'bold in strength'. 'incedit' means 'steps forward'; 'melior' is a comparative, 'better', with the ablatives 'iaculo… sagittis' ('with javelin and light arrows'). The relative clauses run on without a main verb until 'adsint' at 70.

sentences.t:
seu crudo fidit pugnam committere caestu,
cuncti adsint, meritaeque exspectent praemia palmae.
sentences.l:
or in the raw hide-glove trusts to join battle,
let all be present, and of the earned palm await the prizes.
sentences.i: or who trusts himself to fight with the raw-hide gauntlet: let all be there, and wait for the rewards of a well-earned victory.
sentences.n: 'seu' continues the series, 'or (whoever)'; 'fidit' takes the infinitive 'committere' ('trusts to join'); 'crudo… caestu' is an ablative: the 'caestus' is the boxer's glove of hide strips, here 'raw', unworked leather. 'adsint' and 'exspectent' are jussive subjunctives, 'let them be here, let them wait for'; 'meritae' agrees with 'palmae', 'of the earned palm' (genitive), and '-que' joins 'exspectent' to 'adsint', the palm branch being the sign of victory.

sentences.t: Ore favete omnes, et cingite tempora ramis.”
sentences.l: With your mouths be favourable all, and wreathe your brows with branches.”
sentences.i: Keep a reverent silence, all of you, and wreathe your brows with leafy boughs.”
sentences.n: 'Ore favete' is a ritual formula: 'favete' with 'ore' (or 'linguis') means 'keep a reverent silence', as before a rite; the literal 'be favourable with your mouth' means 'say nothing ill-omened'. 'cingite' is an imperative; 'tempora' are the temples of the head, and 'ramis' (ablative) the branches in the wreath. The mark ” closes Aeneas's speech.

sentences.t: Sic fatus, velat materna tempora myrto;
sentences.l: Thus having spoken, he veils the brows with maternal myrtle;
sentences.i: So saying, he veils his brows with his mother's myrtle;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Sic fatus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'for', active in sense: 'having spoken thus'. 'materna… myrto' is an ablative: myrtle is the plant of Venus, Aeneas's mother, so 'maternal'. 'tempora' (accusative plural) is 'the brows, temples'.

sentences.t:
hoc Elymus facit, hoc aevi maturus Acestes,
hoc puer Ascanius, sequitur quos cetera pubes.
sentences.l:
this Elymus does, this Acestes ripe in years,
this the boy Ascanius, whom follows the rest of the youth.
sentences.i: Elymus does the same, and Acestes, ripe in years, and the boy Ascanius, and after them follows the rest of the young men.
sentences.n: 'hoc' is the repeated object of 'facit' (anaphora): 'this (he) does'. 'Elymus' is a Trojan who stayed in Sicily (the Latin Library prints 'Helymus', an orthographic variant). 'aevi maturus' is a genitive of respect, 'mature in age'. 'sequitur quos' has a relative whose antecedent is the three just named: 'whom the rest of the young follow'. 'cetera pubes' is a singular collective, 'the rest of the youth'.

sentences.t:
Ille e concilio multis cum milibus ibat
ad tumulum, magna medius comitante caterva.
sentences.l:
He from the council with many thousands went
to the mound, in the middle, a great crowd accompanying.
sentences.i: He went from the assembly with many thousands to the tomb, with a great throng about him as he walked in the middle.
sentences.n: 'Ille' is Aeneas. 'e concilio' means 'out of the assembly', and 'multis cum milibus' 'with many thousands' ('cum' placed between the adjective and the noun); 'milibus' is an ablative plural. 'ibat' is an imperfect. 'ad tumulum' is the goal, the grave-mound of Anchises. 'magna medius comitante caterva' is an ablative absolute, 'a great crowd accompanying', with 'medius' predicative, 'in the middle'.

sentences.t:
Hic duo rite mero libans carchesia Baccho
fundit humi, duo lacte novo, duo sanguine sacro,
purpureosque iacit flores, ac talia fatur:
sentences.l:
Here two cups duly with pure Bacchus pouring,
he pours on the ground, two with new milk, two with sacred blood,
and scatters purple flowers, and such things says:
sentences.i: Here, as the rite requires, he pours two cups of unmixed wine on the ground, two of fresh milk, two of the blood of the victim, and scatters crimson flowers, and says:
sentences.n: 'Hic' is an adverb, 'here' (at the tomb). 'libans' is a present participle with 'fundit' as the main verb. 'carchesia' is a Greek word (a tall cup) in the accusative plural, with 'duo' agreeing in the neuter plural. 'mero Baccho' is an ablative, 'with pure wine': 'Bacchus' stands for wine (metonymy) and 'merum' is wine undiluted. 'humi' is a locative, 'on the ground'. 'lacte novo' and 'sanguine sacro' are ablatives; the three liquids are the offerings to the dead. 'purpureos' means 'bright red' rather than the modern 'purple'.

sentences.t: “Salve, sancte parens:
sentences.l: “Hail, holy parent:
sentences.i: “Hail, holy father:
sentences.n: The opening mark “ begins Aeneas's address to his father's spirit. 'Salve' is the singular imperative of 'salveo' (a greeting), and 'sancte parens' a vocative. The colon is followed by the same greeting in the plural, to the spirits.

sentences.t:
iterum salvete, recepti
nequiquam cineres, animaeque umbraeque paternae.
sentences.l:
again hail, recovered
in vain ashes, and souls and shades of my father.
sentences.i: and hail again, ashes recovered in vain, and spirit and shade of my father.
sentences.n: 'salvete' is the plural imperative, addressed to 'cineres', 'animae' and 'umbrae', which are the vocatives; 'iterum' means 'a second time'. 'recepti nequiquam cineres' means 'ashes recovered in vain': Aeneas had saved his father from burning Troy, only for Anchises to die in Sicily before Italy was reached. The plurals 'animae', 'umbrae' and 'cineres' are poetic, all for the one dead man. 'paternae' (feminine plural) agrees with both 'animae' and 'umbrae'.

sentences.t:
Non licuit fines Italos fataliaque arva,
nec tecum Ausonium (quicumque est) quaerere Thybrim.”
sentences.l:
It was not permitted the Italian borders and the fated fields,
nor with you the Ausonian (whatever it is) Tiber to seek.”
sentences.i: It was not granted to you to seek with me the borders of Italy and the lands that fate has set, nor the Ausonian Tiber, whatever stream it may be.”
sentences.n: 'Non licuit' is impersonal, 'it was not allowed' (to you, understood), with the infinitive 'quaerere' governing 'fines', 'arva' and 'Thybrim'. 'fataliaque arva' means 'the fated fields', i.e. promised by fate. 'nec tecum' goes with 'quaerere': 'nor with you to seek'. 'Ausonium' means 'Italian' (Ausonia was an old name of southern Italy). 'quicumque est' is a parenthesis meaning 'whatever river it may be'. 'Thybrim' is a Greek-style accusative in -im. The mark ” closes the speech.

sentences.t:
Dixerat haec, adytis cum lubricus anguis ab imis
septem ingens gyros, septena volumina traxit,
amplexus placide tumulum lapsusque per aras,
sentences.l:
He had said these things, when from the depths of the shrine a slippery snake
seven huge coils, seven rings drew out,
embracing the mound peacefully and gliding among the altars,
sentences.i: He had said this when a smooth-gliding snake, huge, from the deepest part of the shrine drew out its seven coils, seven rings of its body, quietly encircling the tomb and sliding among the altars,
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Dixerat' is a pluperfect, followed by 'cum' with the perfect indicative 'traxit': 'he had said… when it drew', the 'cum inversum' which gives the main action to the second clause. 'adytis ab imis' is 'from the lowest parts of the shrine' (the tomb as a chamber). 'septem ingens gyros': 'ingens' agrees with 'anguis' (huge), 'septem' with 'gyros', the accusative plural of a Greek word; 'septena volumina' is in apposition, 'septena' being a distributive used for 'septem'. 'amplexus' and 'lapsus' are perfect participles of deponents, active in sense, 'having embraced' and 'having glided'. 'placide' is an adverb. 'lubricus' is nominative singular masculine with 'anguis'.

sentences.t:
caeruleae cui terga notae, maculosus et auro
squamam incendebat fulgor, ceu nubibus arcus
mille iacit varios adverso sole colores.
sentences.l:
whose backs were of blue marks, and spotted with gold
a gleam lit up its scales, as in the clouds a rainbow
throws a thousand various colours with the sun opposite.
sentences.i: its back was marked with dark blue, and a gleam, flecked with gold, lit up its scales, as when a rainbow in the clouds throws a thousand changing colours, the sun being opposite.
sentences.n: 'caeruleae cui terga notae' has 'cui' as a dative of possession, 'whose', with 'erant' understood (ellipsis): 'whose back had blue marks'; 'notae' (nominative plural) is the subject and 'terga' the plural for the back. 'maculosus et auro… fulgor' means 'a gleam spotted and with gold', 'auro' being an ablative of means or quality with 'maculosus'. 'squamam incendebat' means 'set its scales alight'. 'ceu' is 'as', introducing a simile; 'nubibus' is an ablative of place, 'in the clouds'; 'arcus' is the rainbow, subject of 'iacit'. 'adverso sole' is an ablative absolute, 'the sun being opposite', as a rainbow forms with the sun behind the viewer.

sentences.t: Obstipuit visu Aeneas.
sentences.l: Was stunned at the sight Aeneas.
sentences.i: Aeneas stood stunned at the sight.
sentences.n: 'Obstipuit' is the perfect of 'obstipesco', 'was dumbfounded'; 'visu' is an ablative of the supine, 'at the sight'. The short sentence after the long simile marks the change of pace.

sentences.t:
Ille agmine longo
tandem inter pateras et levia pocula serpens
libavitque dapes, rursusque innoxius imo
successit tumulo, et depasta altaria liquit.
sentences.l:
That one in a long column
at last between the bowls and the smooth cups, the serpent,
tasted the feasts, and again harmless to the bottom
returned to the tomb, and left the altars grazed over.
sentences.i: The serpent, in a long train, made its way at last between the bowls and the smooth cups, tasted the offerings, and went back, harmless, into the depths of the tomb, leaving the altars where it had fed.
sentences.n: 'Ille… serpens' frames the unit, 'that serpent'; 'agmine longo' is an ablative of manner, 'in a long line' (a military word, 'column', for the snake's length). 'pateras' and 'pocula' are the bowls and cups set out for the offerings. 'libavit' is a perfect, 'tasted', in a sacral sense 'took a libation'; 'dapes' are the feast-offerings. 'rursus' means 'again, back'; 'innoxius' is 'harmless'. 'successit tumulo' is a dative with a compound verb, 'went in under the tomb'; 'imo' means 'the lowest'. 'depasta' is a perfect participle of the deponent 'depascor', but here passive in sense, 'grazed upon': the altars the snake had fed on.

sentences.t:
Hoc magis inceptos genitori instaurat honores,
incertus, geniumne loci famulumne parentis
esse putet:
sentences.l:
By this the more the begun to his father he renews the honours,
uncertain whether the genius of the place or the attendant of his parent
he should think it to be:
sentences.i: All the more because of this he takes up again the rites that he had begun for his father, not knowing whether to think it the guardian spirit of the place or the servant of his father:
sentences.n: 'Hoc magis' is an ablative of measure, 'by this the more', 'all the more for this'. 'inceptos' is a perfect participle agreeing with 'honores'; 'genitori' is a dative (of advantage); 'instaurat' means 'renews'. 'incertus' is nominative, 'uncertain'. 'geniumne… famulumne' is a double indirect question with '-ne… -ne' ('whether… or'), and 'putet' is a present subjunctive, 'he should think'. A 'genius loci' is the guardian spirit of a place; 'famulus' is the attendant, so in the second case a servant of the dead.

sentences.t:
caedit binas de more bidentes,
totque sues, totidem nigrantis terga iuvencos;
sentences.l:
he slays two sheep each according to custom,
and as many swine, and as many black-backed steers;
sentences.i: he kills two sheep apiece in the customary way, and as many pigs, and as many black-backed bullocks;
sentences.n: 'caedit' means 'kills' (the verb of sacrifice); 'binas' is distributive, 'two each'; 'de more' is 'according to custom'. 'bidentes' (two-year-old sheep with a pair of conspicuous teeth) is an accusative plural (Greenough's 'bidentes'; The Latin Library prints 'bidentis'). 'totque… totidem' is a pair, 'so many… just as many'. 'nigrantis terga' is an accusative of respect (a 'Greek' accusative), 'black as to the back', with 'nigrantis' an -is accusative plural.

sentences.t:
vinaque fundebat pateris, animamque vocabat
Anchisae magni Manisque Acheronte remissos.
sentences.l:
and wine he poured from bowls, and called up the soul
of great Anchises and his Manes from Acheron sent back.
sentences.i: and he poured wine from the bowls and summoned the spirit of great Anchises and the shades released from Acheron.
sentences.n: 'fundebat' and 'vocabat' are imperfects, the actions going on, 'was pouring… was calling'. 'animam' is the spirit of the dead man, and 'Manis' an accusative plural in -is for 'Manes', 'the shades' (the spirits of the dead). 'Acheronte remissos' is a perfect participle with an ablative of separation: 'sent back from Acheron', a river of the underworld, so the shades allowed back to the upper world for the offering. 'Anchisae magni' is a genitive (-ae, first declension).

sentences.t:
Nec non et socii, quae cuique est copia, laeti
dona ferunt, onerant aras, mactantque iuvencos;
sentences.l:
Nor less also the comrades, according to what is the means of each, glad
bring gifts, load the altars, and slaughter steers;
sentences.i: And the companions too, each as his means allow, bring their gifts gladly, heap the altars, and slay bullocks;
sentences.n: 'Nec non et' is an idiom meaning 'and also, likewise' (a double negative turned into emphasis). 'quae cuique est copia' means 'whatever means each has', a relative clause with the dative of possession 'cuique… est'. 'laeti' is nominative plural, 'glad'. 'ferunt', 'onerant' and 'mactant' are present indicatives in an asyndetic series, 'bring, load, slay'; 'mactant' is the sacrificial word for killing a victim.

sentences.t:
ordine aena locant alii, fusique per herbam
subiciunt veribus prunas et viscera torrent.
sentences.l:
in order bronze vessels some place, and stretched through the grass
under the spits put coals and roast the entrails.
sentences.i: Some set the bronze cauldrons in rows, and others, stretched out on the grass, put hot coals beneath the spits and roast the entrails.
sentences.n: 'alii' is the subject of 'locant' and 'fusi' (also nominative plural) agrees with a second, understood 'alii': 'some… others'. 'aena' is a neuter plural noun, 'bronze vessels', from 'aenum'. 'fusi per herbam' is a perfect participle, 'stretched out through the grass'. 'veribus' is a dative with the compound verb 'subiciunt', 'put under the spits'; 'prunas' means 'live coals'; 'viscera torrent' are the 'entrails', the part of the victim eaten at the feast, which is the closing scene of the part.
